the direct cause of mortality. It could, to the contrary, be an external cause which ends up killing people. There is a much greater chance that the uninsured are allocating a larger segment of their health care spending to preventable services and over-the-counter drugs. I'll accept that trade, just as I would readily allow an alcoholic to drink himself to death provided he ceased injecting substances harmful to his liver at the same time.
And so I'm going to go for another possibility here. To the extent that people avoid small costs, they are healthy and avoid big costs. If individuals are skipping rent payments, they likely also are avoiding preventive colonoscopies. This isn't the sort of cost-benefit tradeoff that affects a disproportionate number of the societies disadvantaged, if for no other reason than that incidence among the societies most disadvantaged is very low. I'm not sure it's irrelevant, though. Renal problems are increasingly common in this population, no doubt a result of less preventative care. The obvious tragedy of the uninsured might be less sensational than a tragic endpoint like death.
